audio: Welcome to Hillside Botanical Gardens. Before you start exploring, let me give you some information. The gardens are divided into four main areas. As you go through the main gate, the Rose Garden is directly in front of you. To your left, you'll find the Tropical House, a large glass building where the temperature is kept at around twenty-eight degrees, so you may want to remove your coat. Behind the Tropical House is the Lake, where you can see ducks and swans, but please don't feed them bread, as it's bad for their health. The newest area is the Japanese Garden, which opened last spring at the far end of the park. Guided tours leave from the café every hour, and they're free with your ticket. The café closes at four thirty, half an hour before the gardens close.

qs.e: «the Rose Garden is directly in front of you».

What time do the gardens close?
qs.e: El café cierra a las 4:30, media hora ANTES: los jardines a las 5:00.

audio: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for coming to this information session about our new recycling scheme. From the first of next month, each household will receive three bins instead of two. The blue bin is for paper and cardboard, the green bin for glass and tins, and the brown bin, which is new, is for food waste. Food waste will be collected every week, while the other bins will be collected every two weeks. Please remember that plastic bags should not go in any of the recycling bins; you can take them to the collection points at supermarkets. If you need a larger bin, for example because you have a big family, you can request one free of charge on the council website.

qs.q: What is the brown bin used for?
qs.e: «the brown bin, which is new, is for food waste».

qs.q: How often will food waste be collected?
Where should people take plastic bags?
How can residents get a larger bin?

audio: Hello, and welcome to your first day as volunteers at the City Food Bank. I'm going to explain how the day works. Your shift starts with a short briefing at nine. After that, most of you will be sorting donations in the warehouse. We check every item for its expiry date; anything that is out of date must be put in the grey containers, not thrown away, because a local farm uses it for animal feed. At around eleven, some of you will move to the front desk to help visitors. Please remember that visitors don't need to explain why they are using the food bank, so don't ask them personal questions. Lunch is provided in the staff room at one o'clock. And finally, if you're interested in becoming a team leader, there's a training course next month; just let Maria know.

qs.q: What happens to out-of-date food?
qs.e: «a local farm uses it for animal feed».

qs.q: What should volunteers avoid doing at the front desk?

qs.e: «in the staff room at one o'clock».

audio: Hi everyone, I'm Tom, and I'll be your guide on today's walking tour of the old town. The tour lasts about two hours, and we'll make one stop for refreshments at the market square. Our first stop is the cathedral, which was built in the twelfth century. Unfortunately, the tower is closed today for repairs, so we can't climb it. After that, we'll walk along the river to the old bridge, which is the oldest stone bridge in the region. Please stay together, especially when crossing roads, and keep your tickets, because they give you a ten percent discount at the city museum.

audio:
M: Dr Evans, could we ask you about our research project on sleep and exam performance?
W: Of course. How's the survey going?
M: We've had about eighty responses, which is fewer than we hoped.
W: Eighty is acceptable for a pilot study, but you should mention the sample size as a limitation.
W: We were also thinking of adding a sleep diary, where students record their sleep for a week.
W: That would give you more reliable data than asking people to remember. But be realistic: many students stop filling in diaries after a few days.
W: Maybe we could send a reminder each morning?
W: That's sensible. Now, in your draft you say that less sleep causes lower marks.
M: Yes, the correlation was quite strong.
W: But a correlation doesn't prove causation. Students who are stressed might sleep less and also perform worse.
M: So we should say that the two are linked, not that one causes the other.
W: Exactly.

qs.q: What does Dr Evans say about the number of responses?
o: It is too small to use
It is acceptable but should be noted as a limitation
It should be doubled before writing
qs.e: «acceptable for a pilot study, but… mention… as a limitation».

qs.q: Why does Dr Evans support the sleep diary?
o: It gives more reliable data than memory
qs.e: «more reliable data than asking people to remember».

qs.q: What problem with diaries does she mention?
o: They take too long to design
qs.e: «many students stop filling in diaries after a few days».

qs.q: What change do the students agree to make to their draft?

audio: Today we're looking at the history of tea. Tea was first consumed in China, where, according to legend, leaves fell into an emperor's boiling water nearly five thousand years ago. For centuries, tea was used mainly as a medicine before it became a daily drink. In the ninth century, Buddhist monks brought tea seeds to Japan, where a formal tea ceremony later developed. Tea reached Europe through Dutch traders in the early seventeenth century. In Britain, it was at first a luxury, partly because of high taxes, and it only became affordable for ordinary people in the eighteenth century, after those taxes were reduced. In the nineteenth century, the British established huge tea plantations in India to reduce their dependence on Chinese supplies. Today, tea is the most widely consumed drink in the world after water.

qs.q: At first, tea in China was used as a ___.
Tea seeds were taken to Japan by ___.
Tea arrived in Europe through ___ traders.
In Britain, tea was expensive because of high ___.
The British created plantations in ___.

audio: In today's lecture I'll discuss how animals navigate over long distances. Many species use more than one method. Homing pigeons, for example, can use the position of the sun, but on cloudy days they rely on the Earth's magnetic field, which they appear to sense through cells containing iron. Sea turtles also use magnetism; young turtles seem to remember the magnetic signature of the beach where they hatched and return there to lay eggs years later. Some birds that migrate at night use the stars, and experiments in planetariums have shown that they orient themselves using the pattern of stars around the North Star. Smell is important too: salmon find their home river by recognising its unique chemical scent. Finally, researchers have recently discovered that some insects, such as dung beetles, can navigate using the Milky Way.

qs.q: On cloudy days, pigeons use the Earth's magnetic ___.
Turtles return to the beach where they ___.
Experiments with night birds were carried out in ___.
Salmon recognise their river by its ___.
Dung beetles can navigate using the Milky ___.

audio: This morning I want to talk about the architecture of traditional Arab houses and how they were designed for a hot climate. Most houses were built around a central courtyard, which created shade and allowed cool air to collect at night. Walls were thick and made of mud brick or stone, which kept the interior cool during the day. Windows facing the street were small and often covered with wooden screens called mashrabiya, which allowed air to flow while providing privacy. In parts of the Gulf, houses also had wind towers, known as barjeel, which caught breezes and directed them down into the rooms. Many modern architects are now studying these techniques to design buildings that need less air conditioning.

qs.q: Houses were built around a central ___.
Walls were made of mud brick or ___.
Wooden screens on windows provided air flow and ___.
Wind towers caught ___ and sent them into rooms.
Modern architects want buildings that need less air ___.

passage:
Let's talk about your hometown.
1. Where is your hometown?
2. What do you like most about it?
3. Has it changed much in recent years?
model:
1. I'm from Valencia, which is the third-largest city in Spain, on the Mediterranean coast.
2. What I like most is the climate. It's mild all year round, so you can go to the beach even in winter, and people spend a lot of time outdoors.
3. Yes, quite a lot. The seafront has been renovated, and there are many more cycle lanes than when I was a child. It's also become much more international, with people from all over the world living there.
tips: Respuestas de 2-3 frases: ni monosílabos ni discursos.
Da una razón o un ejemplo en cada respuesta.
Usa tiempos variados: present perfect para cambios («has become»).

passage:
Let's talk about food.
1. What kind of food do you like?
2. Do you prefer eating at home or eating out?
3. Did you learn to cook when you were young?
model:
1. I really enjoy Middle Eastern food, especially dishes with lots of vegetables and spices, like lentil soup or grilled fish with rice.
2. Generally I prefer eating at home, because it's healthier and cheaper, but I like eating out with friends at weekends to try something different.
3. Not really. My mother did most of the cooking, and I only started cooking properly when I moved out to study. Now I can make a few simple dishes quite well.
tips: «Generally… but…» muestra matiz.
Usa vocabulario concreto (lentil soup, grilled fish).
Responde en pasado cuando la pregunta va en pasado.

passage:
Let's talk about your studies or work.
1. Do you work or are you a student?
2. Why did you choose that job or subject?
3. What would you like to do in the future?
model:
1. At the moment I'm working at a hotel reception, mainly with guests from abroad.
2. I chose it because I love meeting people from different cultures, and I speak several languages, so it seemed like a natural fit.
3. In the future I'd like to work in hotel management, and maybe study tourism to learn the business side properly.
tips: «At the moment I'm…» para la situación actual.
«I'd like to…» / «I'm hoping to…» para el futuro.
Personaliza: los examinadores premian respuestas reales.

passage:
Let's talk about sport.
1. Do you play any sports?
2. What sports are popular in your country?
3. Do you think children should do more sport at school?
model:
1. Yes, I play football most weekends. I usually play in midfield with a local amateur team.
2. Football is by far the most popular, but basketball and padel tennis have become really popular in recent years too.
3. Definitely. Children spend so much time sitting in front of screens that schools should give them more opportunities to be active, not just one or two hours a week.
tips: «by far the most…» es una expresión de banda alta.
Para opinar: «Definitely», «I'd say», «To be honest».
Justifica siempre la opinión.

passage:
Let's talk about weather.
1. What's the weather like where you live?
2. What's your favourite season?
3. Does the weather affect your mood?
model:
1. Right now I live in Tokyo, and the summers are extremely hot and humid, while the winters are fairly dry and cold.
2. My favourite season is autumn, because the temperature is comfortable and the leaves turn red and yellow, which is beautiful.
3. Yes, I think so. When it's sunny I feel more energetic, but long rainy periods make me feel a bit lazy.
tips: Adjetivos precisos: humid, mild, chilly, scorching.
«which is…» para añadir un comentario.
Admite matices: «a bit», «fairly».

passage:
Let's talk about reading.
1. Do you like reading?
2. What did you read when you were a child?
3. Do you prefer paper books or e-books?
model:
1. Yes, I do, although I don't read as much as I'd like because I'm quite busy.
2. As a child I loved adventure stories and comics. I remember reading the same books again and again.
3. I prefer paper books for novels, because I like the feeling of turning the pages, but for studying I use e-books, since I can search for words and carry lots of books on my phone.
tips: «not as much as I'd like» = estructura natural.
«I remember + -ing» para recuerdos.
Contrasta con «but» y razona.

passage:
Let's talk about technology.
1. What piece of technology do you use most?
2. Is there any technology you find difficult to use?
3. How has technology changed the way people communicate?
model:
1. Without a doubt, my smartphone. I use it for everything: messages, maps, translating, and even paying in shops.
2. To be honest, smart TVs confuse me sometimes. Every brand has a different menu, and I often struggle to find the settings I need.
3. It's made communication much faster and cheaper. I can video call my family in Spain for free, which would have been impossible twenty years ago. On the other hand, I think people have fewer face-to-face conversations now.
tips: «would have been impossible» = tercer condicional, puntúa en gramática.
Dos caras: «On the other hand…».
Ejemplos personales concretos.

passage:
Let's talk about friends.
1. Do you prefer having a few close friends or many friends?
2. How do you usually spend time with your friends?
3. Is it easy to make new friends where you live?
model:
1. I'd rather have a few close friends I can trust than lots of people I hardly know.
2. We usually play football together, or go for a walk and get something to eat afterwards.

«It can be a bit challenging» suena natural y matizado.
Explica cómo, no solo sí/no.

passage:
Describe a place you have visited that you would like to visit again.
You should say:
• where it is
• when you went there
• what you did there
and explain why you would like to go back.
model:
I'd like to talk about Kyoto, the old capital of Japan, which is about thirty minutes by train from the city where I live.

The first time I went was in autumn last year, on a long weekend. I went with two friends who were visiting from Spain, so I acted as their guide.

We spent the first day in the eastern part of the city, walking through the narrow streets around Kiyomizu temple. The views over the city were amazing, especially in the late afternoon. On the second day we got up very early to visit the bamboo forest in Arashiyama before the crowds arrived, and then we rented bicycles and rode along the river. We also tried lots of local food, like tofu dishes and green tea sweets.

The reason I'd love to go back is that I feel I only saw a small part of the city. There are hundreds of temples and gardens, and each season gives the city a completely different atmosphere. Next time I'd like to go in spring, during the cherry blossom season, and visit some of the quieter areas in the north, like Ohara. I think Kyoto is the kind of place you could visit ten times and still discover something new.
tips: En el minuto de preparación: 1 palabra clave por punto.
Sigue el orden de la tarjeta: te da estructura gratis.
Termina con la razón: es la parte que más se recuerda.

passage:
Describe a person who has influenced you.
You should say:
• who this person is
• how you know them
• what they have done
and explain how they have influenced you.
model:
The person I'd like to talk about is my football coach when I was a teenager. His name was Manuel, and he coached our local team for about five years.

I met him when I was thirteen and joined the club. At the beginning I wasn't a very good player, and I was quite shy, but he always gave everyone a chance, regardless of their level.

What made him special was that he cared about us as people, not just as players. He used to ask about our studies, and if someone's marks were falling, he would encourage them to spend more time studying, even if it meant missing a training session. He also organised trips to other cities for tournaments, which for many of us was the first time travelling without our families.

He influenced me in two main ways. First, he taught me the value of discipline: turning up on time, training even when you don't feel like it. Second, he showed me that a leader should support everyone, not only the strongest. Now, when I work in a team, I try to follow his example and make sure everyone feels included.
tips: «used to / would» para hábitos pasados.
Dos influencias claras con «First… Second…».
Conecta con tu vida actual al final.

passage:
Describe a skill you would like to learn.
You should say:
• what the skill is
• how you would learn it
• how difficult you think it would be
and explain why you want to learn this skill.
model:
A skill I've wanted to learn for a long time is flying a helicopter.

To learn it, I'd need to enrol in a flight school and take a private pilot's course. This involves both theory classes, such as navigation, meteorology and aviation law, and a minimum number of practical flying hours with an instructor. Ideally, I'd do it in Spain, where there are several well-known schools.

I think it would be quite difficult, for several reasons. Controlling a helicopter requires excellent coordination, because you use both hands and both feet at the same time, and even small movements have big effects. On top of that, the theory exams are demanding, and the course is very expensive, so I'd need to plan my finances carefully.

The main reason I want to learn is that it combines two things I love: technology and travel. Seeing landscapes from the air must be an incredible experience. In addition, I'm interested in tourism, and helicopter tours are becoming popular, so in the long term it could even become part of my career. It's an ambitious goal, but I believe it's achievable if I work towards it step by step.
tips: Condicionales (I'd need, would be) para algo hipotético.
«for several reasons» + lista te organiza.
Vocabulario específico del tema sube la nota de Lexical Resource.

passage:
Describe a gift you gave to someone.
You should say:
• what the gift was
• who you gave it to
• why you chose it
and explain how the person felt about it.
model:
I'd like to describe a gift I gave to my younger brother on his eighteenth birthday. It was a good-quality backpack for travelling.

My brother had just finished school and was planning to travel around Europe by train with some friends during the summer. His old school bag was far too small and quite worn out, so I thought a proper travel backpack would be really practical.

I chose it carefully. I went to an outdoor shop and asked the staff for advice, and I picked one that was light, waterproof and had lots of pockets. I also put a small notebook inside, with a few tips from my own travels and the addresses of some friends he could visit.

He was really surprised and happy when he opened it. He said it was exactly what he needed, and he used it for the whole trip. When he came back, he told me the notebook was the best part, because one of my friends showed them around her city. It made me feel good to know the gift was both useful and personal.
tips: Historia en pasado con detalles concretos.
Añade una sorpresa o anécdota: hace la respuesta memorable.
Termina con tus sentimientos o los del otro.

passage:
Describe a time when you helped someone.
You should say:
• who you helped
• when and where it happened
• how you helped them
and explain how you felt about it.
model:
I'd like to talk about a time I helped a family of tourists who were lost at Osaka Station, which is one of the most confusing stations in Japan.

It happened last spring on a weekday evening. I was on my way home when I noticed a family with two small children looking at their phones and a paper map, clearly stressed. I heard them speaking Spanish, so I asked if they needed help.

It turned out they were trying to find the train to Kyoto, but they had gone to the wrong line twice. I explained the difference between the JR lines and the private railways, showed them which ticket to buy, and walked with them to the correct platform. I also wrote down the name of their station in Japanese so they could show it to staff if they got lost again.

I felt really happy afterwards, because I remembered how confused I felt when I first arrived in Japan. The parents thanked me many times, and the children waved from the train. It was a small thing, but it made my day.
tips: «It turned out (that)…» = conector narrativo natural.
Describe la emoción con un motivo («because I remembered…»).
Mantén el orden cronológico.

passage:
Describe an important decision you made.
You should say:
• what the decision was
• when you made it
• how you made it
and explain whether you think it was the right decision.
model:
One of the most important decisions I've ever made was moving to Japan to work and study for a few years.

I made the decision about three years ago, after finishing my studies. I'd always been interested in Japanese culture, and I felt that if I didn't do it then, I probably never would.

It wasn't an easy decision. I spent several months researching visas, the cost of living and possible jobs. I also talked to people who had lived in Japan, both through online forums and friends of friends. I made a list of pros and cons: on the one hand, I'd be far from my family and I didn't speak Japanese well; on the other, I'd gain international experience and learn a new language.

Looking back, I'm convinced it was the right choice. It hasn't always been easy, especially at the beginning, when I felt lonely and struggled with the language. Let's discuss tourism.
1. What are the benefits of tourism for a city?
2. Can tourism have negative effects on local people?
3. How might tourism change in the future?
model:
1. The most obvious benefit is economic. Tourism creates jobs in hotels, restaurants and transport, and it brings money into local businesses. It can also encourage cities to protect their historic buildings and improve infrastructure.
2. Yes, definitely. In very popular places, rents can rise because apartments are turned into holiday rentals, so local people are pushed out. Overcrowding is another issue: residents in cities like Kyoto sometimes can't even get on a bus because they're full of tourists.
3. I think there'll be a shift towards more sustainable and spread-out tourism. Governments may introduce limits or entry fees for crowded areas, and technology might help tourists choose less busy times and places. I also expect more people to look for authentic local experiences rather than just famous landmarks.

Para el futuro: «I expect», «there'll be a shift towards», «might».

passage:
Let's discuss education and technology.
1. Can online learning replace teachers?
2. What skills will young people need in the future?
3. Should schools teach practical life skills such as managing money?
model:
1. I don't think it can replace them completely. Online platforms are excellent for practising and for accessing information, but teachers do much more than transmit knowledge. They motivate students, notice when someone is struggling and help develop social skills. The best model is probably a blend of both.
2. Apart from digital literacy, I'd say adaptability is crucial, because many of today's jobs may not exist in twenty years. Communication skills and the ability to work with people from different cultures will also be increasingly important in a globalised world.
3. Absolutely. Many young people leave school without knowing how to make a budget or understand a contract. Teaching basic financial planning, how to save and how to avoid debt would prevent many problems later in life.
tips: Matiza: «I don't think it can replace them completely».
«Apart from…, I'd say…» organiza ideas.
Ideas generales + consecuencia («would prevent…»).

passage:
Let's discuss the environment.
1. Who should be responsible for protecting the environment?
2. Do you think people in your country are environmentally aware?
3. What can cities do to reduce pollution?
model:
1. I think it's a shared responsibility, but governments and large companies have the greatest power. They can pass laws and change how products are made. Individuals matter too, though, because small changes multiplied by millions of people make a difference.
2. Generally speaking, yes, especially younger people. Recycling is very common, and people are increasingly using public transport or cycling. However, there's still a lot of single-use plastic, particularly in supermarkets.
3. Cities can invest in reliable public transport, create more cycle lanes and pedestrian areas, and plant more trees. Some cities have also introduced low-emission zones where older, polluting vehicles aren't allowed, which seems to work quite well.
tips: «Generally speaking» para generalizar.
Concede y contrasta: «However, there's still…».
Ofrece varias soluciones concretas.
